title: How I used AI to build Death Bag: 4,000 hours of work, and definitely not one prompt
author: Suspicious_Neck_4069
selftext:
I've been making games professionally for around 10 years, and one thing hasn't changed with AI:

Making an actual commercial game still takes an absurd amount of work.

Death Bag has been in production for roughly 9 months. I've been working around 15 hours a day for most of that period, which puts my personal development time somewhere around 4,000 hours. And that's with AI. Without it, considering the amount of programming, 3D production, concept work, UI, audio, voices, music, iteration and debugging involved, I estimate the same production would represent something closer to 20,000 hours of traditional human work, or, more realistically, a small team instead of one developer.

That's the part of AI game development I don't think gets shown enough. Here, my actual production pipeline :

**Programming** : Codex + Unity/MCP

Codex is connected directly to my Unity project through MCP. I use it for gameplay programming, prototyping systems, editor tools, debugging, refactoring and iteration. This has probably been the single biggest productivity multiplier in the project. But there's still a huge difference between generating code and shipping a working interconnected game. A system has to interact correctly with dozens of other systems, survive edge cases, work with the UI, save/load correctly, remain maintainable and, most importantly, actually be fun. A lot of the work is still deciding what should exist, testing it, finding out why it doesn't work, and iterating.

**2D concepts for characters, environments, props and UI** : GPT Image + Nano Banana Pro

For image generation, I mainly use GPT Image and Nano Banana Pro. I use them for: characters in T-pose as a base for 3D generation, environment concepts, props, UI elements, icons, visual exploration.The important part for me is that these images are usually not the final asset by themselves. They're often the starting point of another stage in the pipeline.

**2D Cleanup** : Photoshop - NOT AI

It is an essential, indispensable step: I retouch anything that might be considered "slop." I use the exact same process as if the image had been created by a human, applying the same high standards.

**2D to 3D** : Tripo AI

Some retouched concepts are then passed through TripoAI to create a first 3D model. This can save an enormous amount of blocking/modeling time. The output, however, is rarely something I can simply drag into Unity and ship, even though it's happening more and more often with the new updates. Not game-ready right now, but close.

**3D cleanup** : Blender / Cinema 4D - NOT AI

This is still traditional manual work. Depending on the asset: geometry cleanup, topology, proportions, UVs, materials, mesh corrections, separating objects (can be do with tripo), fixing AI-generated artifacts, optimization, preparing models for rigging/game use,

**Rigging** : AccuRig

Characters are prepared and rigged through AccuRig, usually after manual cleanup.

**Animation** : Mixamo / Asset Store / custom work - mostly NOT AI

Animations are currently a combination of: Mixamo, Unity Asset Store, my own animation work, manual modifications/integration. Then everything still needs to be configured and tested inside the game.

**Voice acting / voices** : ElevenLabs

I use ElevenLabs for character voices and voice-over. This lets me iterate very quickly on characters, performances and tone without needing a recording pipeline for every prototype.

**Music / songs** : Suno

Suno is used for music and songs.



The biggest misconception I've encountered is that AI somehow removes the work but It doesn't. What it does is reduce the cost of production dramatically. Death Bag has around 120 unique 3D characters. If I had created all of them myself using a traditional workflow, I estimate it would have taken me roughly two years just for the characters. Hiring 3D artists would have cost me somewhere around $40,000 (money I simply don't have).

So without AI, this scope wouldn't have been “more difficult”. It simply wouldn't have existed.

But AI doesn't remove the human workload either. In a weird way, it can actually make you work more. A lot of people who use these tools seriously will probably recognize this: AI increases your production capacity so much that you constantly try to keep up with it. And I can't. Even working around 15 hours a day, the tools can produce ideas, code, assets and possibilities faster than I can review, fix, integrate and polish them. So instead of using AI to make the same game in 1/5th of the time, I ended up using it to make a much larger game in roughly the same insane amount of time I'd normally spend developing.

All That is very different from the “one-prompt game” narrative. And to me, that's where AI-assisted game development gets genuinely interesting.



Has AI actually reduced the amount of time you work? Or has it mostly increased the amount of things you're now crazy enough to try building?

replies.author: Suspicious_Neck_4069
replies.body:
Hi, it’s roughly 4,000 hours of total production over about 9 months. The scope probably explains where a lot of that time went:

\-240 tokens, each with its own gameplay function.

\-Each combat-related token also needs its corresponding in-game animation/visual behavior. That part still lacks polish in the trailer, precisely because there’s a ridiculous amount of it to produce, but it’s on the roadmap.

\-120 unique 3D characters, all prepared to support real-time slicing/dismemberment.

\-12 environments.

\-Around 10 scripted story sequences, on top of the actual deckbuilding/combat loop.

Then there’s all the less visible stuff: programming the systems, AI behavior, UI, progression, save system, balancing, 3D cleanup, rigging, animation setup, materials, audio, voices, music, integration, optimization, bug fixing, Steam integration, trailer production, etc.

And probably the biggest time sink of all: iteration. Build something → test it → realize it doesn’t work → change the design → break three other systems → fix them → test again → eventually throw the whole thing away and rebuild it 😄

AI makes individual parts dramatically faster to produce, but when you’re trying to turn all those parts into an actual commercial game, there’s still an enormous amount of human work between “generated” and “shippable.” So the \~4,000h is the accumulation of hundreds of systems/assets/features that all need to actually work together.

comments.author: chicharro_frito
comments.body: Thanks for sharing your journey! How much $$ have you spent on AI?

replies.author: Suspicious_Neck_4069
replies.body:
Surprisingly little, actually almost embarrassingly little 😅

In terms of AI tools specifically:

\-ChatGPT: $20/month, although I’ve had that subscription for years, so I don’t really count it as a Death Bag-specific expense

\-TripoAI: \~$60 (3 months)

\-Suno: \~$30 (3 months)

\-ElevenLabs: \~$30 (3 months)

So roughly $120 in additional AI expenses specifically for the game. If I count 9 months of ChatGPT too, it’s around $300 total. Then there’s the $100 Steam fee, but obviously that’s not AI-related. Photoshop too. I’m almost ashamed of how small that number is compared to the amount of content produced. That said, I’ve also been developing games for around 10 years, so I’ve accumulated a ridiculous library of assets, music, animations, tools, plugins, sound effects, and various other resources over time.
